title: How to learn frontend (and keep improving)

plan.summary: A repeatable system for learning frontend: read primary sources, build small demos, measure them in DevTools, explain them, and check browser support before shipping.

prerequisites.bridge: DevTools let you inspect and measure a live page.
WHATWG and W3C write the specs that browsers implement.
Git tracks code changes; GitHub hosts repositories and issues.

outcomes: Explain the read, build, measure, explain loop and run it on one feature.
Explain why primary sources beat tutorials, and find the right spec section.
Decide whether a web feature can ship today using Baseline and caniuse.
Build a feature check that falls back when an API is missing.
Build a weekly routine of practice, news, code reading and teaching.

lesson_outline.title: The learning loop: read, build, measure, explain
lesson_outline.visual_reason: The four-step loop is the roadmap's own convention; no vetted source states it, so a worked prose trace plus OrderSteps practice is used instead of a drawn cycle.

experience.override_reason: The cycle is the roadmap convention without a vetted source, so no video may draw it.

lesson_outline.title: Primary sources over tutorials
lesson_outline.visual_reason: TC39 stages 0 to 4 are an ordered maturity sequence stated by the process document.
lesson_outline.interaction_goal: Step through the stages and say at which stage a feature is safe to rely on.

lesson_outline.title: Can I ship it? Baseline and caniuse
lesson_outline.visual_reason: Baseline status changes when browser support and elapsed months change; the learner changes them and watches the label move.
lesson_outline.interaction_goal: Toggle core-browser support and months since newly available; predict the Baseline label.

lesson_outline.title: Feature detection, polyfills and experimental features
lesson_outline.visual_reason: Toggling simulated browser support and watching which branch of the detection code runs shows progressive enhancement directly.
lesson_outline.interaction_goal: Turn an API on or off in a simulated browser and predict which code path renders.

lesson_outline.title: Read other people's code
lesson_outline.visual_reason: Stepping line by line through real Preact source shows how to read a library.
lesson_outline.interaction_goal: Step through a small Preact source function and predict the value it returns.

experience.override_reason: CodeWalkthrough already steps through the code line by line, so a separate video adds no learning value.

lesson_outline.title: A weekly routine: practice and staying current
lesson_outline.visual_reason: A basic routine needs a short list and a sorting activity, not a drawing; cadences are roadmap advice, not sourced data.

lesson_outline.title: Build in public and teach
lesson_outline.visual_reason: The GitHub Open Source Guide gives an ordered path to a first contribution; a diagram shows it.
lesson_outline.interaction_goal: Trace a first contribution from README and CONTRIBUTING to issue to pull request.

mini_projects.use_case: A frontend team lead pastes a list of CSS and JS features and gets each one's support and Baseline-style status from MDN browser-compat-data, to decide what can ship without fallbacks.
A blog adds a Share button that uses the Web Share API where it exists and falls back to copy-to-clipboard everywhere else.

capstone.name: TIL learning journal
capstone.problem: A developer working through a long roadmap needs one web app to log a today-I-learned note per item, link its primary sources, show the Baseline status of web features it mentions, and surface notes due for review.

goals: master frontend engineering end to end from the N1 roadmap
learn visually and by experimenting with simulations
keep improving after the roadmap ends

curriculum.scope: How a developer learns frontend and keeps improving: the learning loop, primary sources, browser support literacy, feature detection, staying current, practice, code reading and teaching.
